extracted.intended_audience: cartoonists, humor writers, editors, and general readers interested in the psychology and craft of cartoon humor
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and practical criteria used by a New Yorker cartoon editor for selecting, adapting, and judging cartoons and captions (including caption-contest selection and editorial curation). Emphasizes cognitive "get it" moments, sources of material, visual positioning, categorization, and use of crowdsourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual positioning / character dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: Switch the position so that the guy saying it is in a position of superiority ... because it makes it funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting a line into a cartoon, change the visual relationship between characters (who's dominant, who’s subordinate) to increase comedic effect; the example: turning a snotty phone quip into a cartoon by placing the speaker in a position of superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embarrassment as comedic material
rubrics_metrics.description: Embarrassment is the mother's milk of humor. Embarrassment at one time, humor later. Anything that's embarrassing is potentially funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on awkward, guilty, or anxiety-filled personal or cultural moments as raw material for humor; these themes often translate into relatable, funny cartoons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source: real-life voice and exasperation
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea came to him during a phone call with a 'friend' who couldn't seem to find the time to get together ... I got exasperated with him and said, 'How about never? Is never good for you?' So, it was really a snotty line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic conversational lines and real emotional reactions (exasperation, snottiness) can be strong seeds for captions; adapt wording and perspective to maximize punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create an identifiable 'get it' (a-ha) cognitive moment
rubrics_metrics.description: We watched their eyes and the moment that they get the cartoon their pupil expands almost like it would for a flashbulb. So we can track the actual 'get it moment.' ... humor is a cognitive process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design cartoons so the viewer experiences a clear instant of recognition or surprise (‘a-ha’). Clarity of setup and payoff that triggers that cognitive reaction is crucial; attention and eye movement patterns can indicate success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for wide variability in audience response
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor itself and your response to humor — that's one of the things I learned ... is very, very, varied and there's a huge amount of variability between subjects and there's even great variability within a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect diverse reactions across people and contexts; do not assume uniform taste. Use iterative feedback to find broadly appealing material or to target a specific niche audience deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorize joke mechanisms to inform selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually it's my assistant ... categorizes them in all the different ways the jokes are made and I pick, maybe [10 or so.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically sort submissions by joke type/mechanism (e.g., verbal gag, visual twist, irony, embarrassment-based) to ensure a range of approaches and to identify strong examples within each category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use crowdsourcing / editor polling for final choice
rubrics_metrics.description: I use SurveyMonkey and I send it out to the New Yorker editors and ... the responses incredibly vary. At that point, it's this crowdsourcing. You know what? I'll tend to go with the one the crowd likes at that point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After narrowing down candidates, poll a representative group of editors or readers to see which version resonates most; favor the crowd-favorite as a pragmatic editorial decision when reactions vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-volume curation and staged narrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: He evaluates more than 500 cartoons submitted to the magazine each week. What we do is after we look through all 5,000 [submissions] ... I pick, maybe [10 or so.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operate a multi-stage selection pipeline: initial broad review to filter large volume, categorize and select a small set of finalists, then use polling/editorial review to choose the published cartoon(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay of visual and verbal elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the cartoons were just verbal cartoons and sometimes they had a visual element and we watched their eyes ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how visuals and captions work together; some jokes rely primarily on text, others on the image or the interaction between them. Visual framing can guide the viewer toward the punchline and enhance the 'get it' moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/personal specificity as material
rubrics_metrics.description: I think what Jewish culture taught me ... is all these embarrassing things, all these guilt-filled things, all these anxiety-filled things are material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage cultural specifics or personal background as comedic fuel; such specificity can yield unique angles but be mindful of audience familiarity and sensitivity.
